title: streaming-sse-chunking-backpressure-debug-notes-nina-park
content:
Context:
- Personal scratchpad for the streaming SSE / chunking / backpressure flakiness we've been seeing in prod (and reproducible locally).
- Symptoms: client (browser + server-side consumers) sometimes receives large pauses (~3-8s) in event arrival even though backend is generating tokens steadily. When pause ends, multiple SSE events arrive 'batched' together in a single chunk.

Hypothesis summary:
1) Upstream batching + missing flush: runtime batches tokens for efficiency but doesn't flush small-enough chunks quickly; HTTP stack coalesces them into bigger TCP segments.
2) Nginx / reverse proxy buffering (proxy_buffering on) or chunked->gzip interactions.
3) Client-side backpressure: fetch()/EventSource read loop is blocked (synchronous work) and then processes backlog in one go.
4) Runtime pauses due to GC / scheduling (Python/Go) causing token generation stalls, so events truly delayed.

Repro notes (local):
- Repro environment: local dev server (node proxy -> python inference shim) and direct runtime (grpc -> runtime) both show similar issues.
- Minimal repro commands I used below.

Curl + no-buffer (basic check):
1) curl -s -N -H "Accept: text/event-stream" http://localhost:8080/stream?model=test-model
   - Observed: sometimes silent for ~4s then many "data: ...
" lines print at once.
2) curl -v -s -N http://localhost:8080/stream?model=test-model 2>&1 | sed -n '1,200p'
   - Look for "Transfer-Encoding: chunked" and keep-alive.

HTTPie (shows buffering differences):
- http --stream GET http://localhost:8080/stream?model=test-model

Python requests (stream=True):
- python3 -c "import requests; r=requests.get('http://localhost:8080/stream?model=test-model', stream=True);
  import sys
  for line in r.iter_lines(decode_unicode=True):
    if line: print('LINE>', line)
    sys.stdout.flush()"

Node fetch (server-side consumer):
- node fetch example I used to reproduce client backpressure scheduling:
  const res = await fetch('http://localhost:8080/stream');
  const reader = res.body.getReader();
  while(true){ const {value, done} = await reader.read(); if(done) break; console.log('chunk len', value && value.length); }

Observed patterns: 
- "chunk len" spikes (e.g., 9000 bytes) after a gap, even though the runtime was emitting 512-1024 byte payloads per token.
- When reproducing behind nginx (local), toggling proxy_buffering off reduces batching but doesn't fully remove the pauses.
- With direct connection to runtime (no nginx), pauses still happen sometimes (lower frequency).

Error / log snippets (copied from runtime / proxy logs):
- runtime log (INFO): "emit_token: took=120ms token_idx=34"
- runtime log (WARN): "kv-cache flush pause: 2.1s"
- proxy log (info): "upstream timed out while reading response header from upstream" (rare)
- client console: "EventSource connection lost, reconnecting..." followed by rapid arrival of many events.

Things I've tried (commands & config):
- Disabled nginx gzip (gzip off) -> small improvement.
- Set proxy_buffering off in nginx -> fewer large chunks, still occasional pauses.
- Changed runtime to call fflush after every "data: ...
"

  (python example)
  sys.stdout.write(f'data: {payload}\n\n')
  sys.stdout.flush()

  -> measurable effect when running as a pure process piping to curl, but in production the runtime writes to a socket and the socket write may be buffered by OS.

- Lowered batching thresholds in runtime (batch size 8->4, time window 200ms->50ms) -> reduced frequency but increased CPU.
- Forced send of empty comment events as keepalive every 200ms: ":


" -> clients stayed connected but still saw batched events after keepalive gap.

Hypotheses to test next (actionable):
- Instrument TCP-level timing on the production instance (tcpdump) to confirm if delays are at the app layer or due to network/proxy buffering.
- Add per-event flush on the runtime socket write path (if possible without huge perf hit) and test latency tradeoffs.
- Try disabling kernel-level coalescing by setting TCP_CORK/TCP_NODELAY appropriately on the runtime socket. (Linux: set TCP_NODELAY=1 to disable Nagle for low-latency small writes)
- Verify runtime thread scheduling / GC: run with pprof or py-spy to find 100-300ms pauses.

Minimal local repro (rough):
1) Start a tiny server that writes an event every 150ms but intentionally sleeps 2s at token 20.
   - python server (Flask + streaming):
     from flask import Flask, Response
     import time
     app = Flask('sse-demo')
     def gen():
         for i in range(50):
             if i==20: time.sleep(2)  # simulate compute pause
             yield f'data: token-{i}\n\n'
             # no explicit flush here (WSGI server may buffer)
     @app.route('/stream')
     def stream():
         return Response(gen(), mimetype='text/event-stream')

2) curl -s -N http://localhost:5000/stream and watch the behavior.

Notes for infra / runtime owners:
- If you can add a small diagnostic endpoint that emits token timestamps (json-lines) from the runtime side that would greatly help isolate where pausing occurs.
- Consider adding an opt-in low-latency mode that sets TCP_NODELAY and aggressively flushes small writes for customers using streaming SLOs.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Q: Are there specific models / sequence lengths where this is more common? Anecdotally more frequent for long-seq (>=1024) responses. Need more telemetry.
- Q: Does our HTTP gateway (k8s ingress / ALB / nginx) re-chunk responses after they leave the pod? Check ingress controller config and service mesh (if present).
- TODO: Run tcpdump + wireshark on a repro to inspect packet-level timing. (blocked on infra access).
- TODO: Add a lightweight instrumented client to capture arrival timestamps in production for a small % of traffic.

Notes-to-self: keep this doc informal; copy polished findings to a Confluence post with exact benchmarks and perf tradeoffs once we have solid tcpdump evidence.

References / quick links:
- GH issue: GH-issue#456 (runtime sse flush)
- Confluence draft: CONFLUENCE-1234

-- Nina
